questions.question: What is federalism?
choices: Division of Congress into two chambers
Direct voting on every national law
Rule by a single unelected leader
Division of power between national and state governments

questions.question: What are delegated powers?
choices: Powers granted to the federal government
Powers retained only by private businesses
Powers used only by city councils
Powers prohibited to every government

questions.question: What are reserved powers?
choices: Powers assigned only to federal courts
Powers delegated exclusively to foreign governments
Powers retained by states or the people under the constitutional framework
Powers exercised only during presidential campaigns

questions.question: What are concurrent powers?
choices: Powers that no government may exercise
Powers exercised by both national and state governments
Powers held only by Congress
Powers belonging only to the president

questions.question: Which amendment addresses powers not delegated to the United States nor prohibited to states?
choices: Tenth Amendment
First Amendment
Fifth Amendment
Nineteenth Amendment

questions.question: Which clause makes the Constitution and valid federal law supreme over conflicting state law?
choices: Establishment Clause
Free Exercise Clause
Appointments Clause
Supremacy Clause

questions.question: Which institution ordinarily has authority to coin U.S. money?
choices: Each state government separately
Every county government
Federal government
Every school district

questions.question: Why does federalism differ from separation of powers?
choices: Federalism divides authority by level; separation of powers divides it by branch
Federalism divides authority by branch; separation of powers divides it by level
Federalism divides authority by region; separation of powers divides it by population
Federalism divides authority by population; separation of powers divides it by region

questions.question: Why can education policies vary among states?
choices: States have substantial authority over education
The Constitution requires identical curricula nationwide
Local schools operate outside all law
Federal courts write every school textbook

questions.question: How can federal grants affect state policy?
choices: Grants automatically abolish state legislatures
Every grant transfers all state powers to Congress
Grants prohibit states from collecting taxes
Funding conditions can encourage states to pursue federal goals within legal limits

questions.question: Why can both states and the federal government collect taxes?
choices: Only states possess constitutional taxing authority
Only the president may authorize state taxes
Taxation is a concurrent power
Local governments cannot collect any revenue

questions.question: What does the Full Faith and Credit Clause generally require?
choices: States to use identical criminal codes
States to recognize other states' public acts, records, and judicial proceedings under applicable rules
States to surrender all court authority to Congress
States to hold every election on the same day

questions.question: Why does federalism allow policy experimentation?
choices: Different states can try different approaches within constitutional limits
States can ignore all constitutional rights
Every state must adopt every other state's policy
Only national officials can propose local policies

questions.question: What constrains state authority in the federal system?
choices: Only the personal preferences of governors
Only the laws of neighboring states
No legal limits once a state joins the Union
The U.S. Constitution and valid federal law

questions.question: Why are interstate disputes sometimes heard by federal courts?
choices: State governments have no courts
Congress cannot regulate any interstate activity
The federal system provides a forum beyond either disputing state's courts
Every interstate dispute must be decided by referendum

questions.question: A state and the federal government both tax income. What kind of power is illustrated?
choices: Reserved power exclusively
Concurrent power
Delegated power exclusively
A prohibited power

questions.question: A state law conflicts with a constitutionally valid federal law. Which principle generally controls?
choices: Federal supremacy
State sovereignty without limits
Municipal home rule
Executive privilege

questions.question: A state establishes licensing rules for teachers. Which authority does this most closely illustrate?
choices: Federal treaty power
Presidential pardon power
Congressional coinage power
State responsibility over education

questions.question: Which comparison is accurate?
choices: A federal system shares authority by level; a unitary system concentrates ultimate authority nationally
A federal system concentrates ultimate authority nationally; a unitary system shares authority constitutionally by level
A federal system makes local officials hereditary; a unitary system requires their direct election
A federal system permits only national courts; a unitary system permits only regional courts

questions.question: Why should a student examine both national and state law when researching a policy?
choices: State law always overrides the Constitution
Authority may be shared and the laws may interact
Federal law regulates only foreign affairs
Local issues never involve federal rights
